name: Stoicism
summary: Stoicism is the Hellenistic school founded by Zeno of Citium around 300 BCE, holding that virtue is the only good and that all rational beings share one law of reason and one world city. Its political thought is about duty: a wise person takes part in public life to serve the common good, rulers must be just, law is right reason and an unjust law is no law, and every human is owed justice. It never set out a programme of policies, and its sources are silent on most modern questions.
scope: Stoicism as a philosophy, read through its own texts and the scholarship on its politics: the early school as reported by Diogenes Laertius, Cicero's De Officiis (following Panaetius), Seneca, Musonius Rufus, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius, with Gill and the Stanford and Internet encyclopedias on cosmopolitanism, law and political engagement. Zeno's lost Republic is used only where Diogenes Laertius reports it. Modern Stoicism is not used for positions; modern policy questions the texts do not address are null.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Diogenes Laertius records the early Stoic doctrine that the best form of government is a mixture of democracy, kingship and aristocracy, and Cicero's De Officiis, which follows the Stoic Panaetius, defends the mixed Roman republic; Seneca instead calls monarchy the best government, so it is not held with full force.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Stoic sources accept good kingship: Musonius says a king should study philosophy and be a living law, Marcus Aurelius admired a kingdom that values the welfare of the governed, Seneca calls monarchy the best government and points to legitimate kings who passed power to their children (On Clemency), and Gill notes Stoics did not reject sole rule, only its abuse.

democracy-best.rationale: Where Stoic sources name a best constitution it is a mixture of democracy, kingship and aristocracy (Diogenes Laertius) or monarchy (Seneca), so democracy alone as the best form contradicts what they state; none argues for rule by the voters as such.

natural-rulers.rationale: Early Stoics held that only the wise know good and evil and so only they are fit to be rulers, magistrates and judges (Diogenes Laertius), and Musonius says a good king needs a superior nature and the best education; fitness to rule is a matter of virtue, not birth.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Diogenes Laertius reports Chrysippus's teaching that the wise man will take part in politics unless something hinders him, because he is made for society and action, and Cicero's Stoic-influenced De Officiis counts scorn for public office as discreditable; Seneca's allowance of retirement is a hindered exception.

state-harmful.rationale: The Stoics define the cosmos and the city by law, hold the wise should take part in politics to restrain vice, and Musonius and Cicero treat kings, magistrates and law as serving justice; only Zeno's early Republic, which dispensed with law-courts and money, points the other way.

single-common-good.rationale: Cicero, following Panaetius, says a statesman must serve the whole citizen body like a trustee, that favouring one part brings party strife, and that the highest statesmanship is not to divide the interests of the citizens but to unite them on impartial justice; Musonius likewise speaks of the common good.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: The Stoics hold that the only law worthy of the name is right reason, which exists by nature and not by convention (Diogenes Laertius, the Stanford article on Seneca), and Musonius says refusing an unjust or shameful order from a father, archon or tyrant is not disobedience. Cicero's On the Laws I says popular votes and decrees could not make robbery or forgery right.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Cicero says the laws and customs of a state are themselves rules of duty and that Socrates's departures from them were an exception, but Musonius says no one need obey an unjust order; the sources tie obedience to the justice of the law, not to its being law.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Cicero and Marcus Aurelius honour those who killed or opposed tyrants (Cato, Brutus, Thrasea, Helvidius), while Seneca calls Brutus mistaken to fear monarchy, so Stoic writers disagree on resisting a ruler.

political-violence-never.rationale: Cicero's De Officiis says there is no fellowship with a tyrant, that killing him is morally right and that such monsters should be cut off from human society; Stoic writers also accept just war and execution, so no source holds violence never justified.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Marcus Aurelius thanks his brother for the idea of an equal commonwealth governed by justice and equality, Seneca tells his friend that slaves are men and comrades, and the Stoic school holds all rational beings share one law and one world city; the school left slavery in place. Cicero's On the Laws I adds that all people share one nature and reason; none of these texts states equal legal rights.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Epictetus defines freedom as having everything happen as one wills with no one able to hinder it, which Stoics hold a slave or prisoner can possess, so a person subject to arbitrary power can still be free in their sense.

traditional-family.rationale: Cicero, following Panaetius, calls marriage the first bond of society and the household the seed-bed of the commonwealth, and Musonius argues marriage and children serve the city and the common good; they describe a husband, wife and children, not other family forms.

abortion-legal.rationale: Musonius praises the lawgivers who forbade abortion and penalised childlessness and calls limiting a family sinful, and Seneca praises his mother for never destroying an unborn child as many women did; no Stoic source argues for legal abortion.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Musonius approves the old lawgivers who rewarded large families and penalised childlessness and says avoiding children wrongs the city; his lecture says nothing about immigration.

premarital-sex.rationale: Musonius and Epictetus limit sex to marriage for both sexes, but the early Stoics Zeno and Chrysippus taught a community of wives with free choice of partners among the wise, so the school gives opposite answers.

filial-duty.rationale: Diogenes Laertius says the Stoics approve honouring parents next after the gods, and Epictetus's Enchiridion says duty to a father means taking care of him, deferring to him and bearing his reproaches, even a bad father; Musonius excepts only wrong orders.

duties-before-rights.rationale: De Officiis builds ethics on duties, says we are not born for ourselves alone because our country claims a share of us, and ranks country first among our obligations; the Stoics do not use the language of individual rights.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Only virtue is good for the Stoics, and Cicero's On the Laws (a Stoic account, per the IEP) says people who do good for private advantage are cunning rather than good and that virtue measured by profit is a kind of vice.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Cicero makes generosity a part of justice, with duty to use wealth for as many as possible within one's means and to the worthy, and Seneca's On Benefits treats helping others as a core duty; they do not require support of the poor as a class.

universal-morality.rationale: The Stoics teach that reason is common to all people, so the law bidding what to do and avoid is common to all (Marcus Aurelius), and that justice and law exist by nature and not by convention (Diogenes Laertius); natural law theory is traced to them. Cicero's On the Laws I grounds justice in nature and not in opinion.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Cicero's On the Laws I says nothing is so alike as man to man, that one definition fits the whole race, that reason is common to all and that man is born for justice by nature and not by opinion; Musonius and Marcus Aurelius likewise say reason is common to all, and the Stoics tell us to live in agreement with that nature.

reason-over-faith.rationale: The Stoics make reason the guide of action and call passions false judgements to be mastered (Diogenes Laertius, Epictetus), but they also teach prayer, sacrifice and divination, so faith has a place alongside reason.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: The Stoics hold that the sage's knowledge rests on cognitive impressions that reliably match reality, and Marcus Aurelius treats common opinion as error to be examined by reason, not as a product of power.

property-fundamental.rationale: Cicero, following Panaetius, says the chief purpose of states was to secure private property and that agrarian laws and cancelling debts destroy equity, while also saying property is private by law or occupation and not by nature; Zeno's Republic wanted no currency.

land-redistribution.rationale: Cicero's De Officiis condemns agrarian laws that drive occupants from their land as undermining the commonwealth and destroying harmony and equity; no Stoic text in the sources argues for redistribution.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Cicero condemns Philippus's call for an equal distribution of property as the most ruinous policy imaginable, and the Stoics hold that wealth is an indifferent, with equality only in virtue.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Cicero says property becomes private by occupation or law and that common things go to common use, but also that securing property is the chief purpose of the state; the Stoic sources do not settle which governs.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Stoics treat wealth, status and luxury as indifferents and warn they enslave; Seneca writes that the man who craves more is poor, Musonius lectures against costly clothing, housing and furnishings, and Marcus Aurelius thanks his teacher for not needing many things.

simple-living.rationale: Musonius's lectures on clothing, shelter and furnishings recommend plain living, Seneca says whoever has made a fair compact with poverty is rich, and Marcus Aurelius learned not to need many things; Seneca's and Marcus's own wealth tempers the record.

death-penalty.rationale: Seneca's On Anger says a judge punishes to reform, or to remove those who cannot be reformed, and executes some publicly to deter others, and the early Stoics held the wise never relax the penalties fixed by law; no Stoic source opposes capital punishment.

rehabilitation.rationale: Seneca, quoting Plato, says punishment looks to the future, one kind aiming to make bad men better and another to put them out of the way, so a Stoic judge does not punish for the past; deterrence and removal also count, and prisons are not discussed.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: The early Stoics held that the wise never relax the penalties fixed by law and ascribe no equity to the sage, whereas Seneca's On Anger has the judge weigh intent and circumstance so equal faults do not get equal penalties.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Seneca's On Anger answers the objection about a murdered father by saying the good man will avenge or protect him out of duty and without anger, so defending others by force is not wrong in itself for a Stoic.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Cicero reports the Stoic doctrine that everything the earth produces is created for human use, and Diogenes Laertius that no question of right arises between humans and animals, so nature is valued by its use to rational beings.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Diogenes Laertius records the Stoic doctrine that there can be no question of right between humans and lower animals because of their unlikeness, and the Stanford article notes Augustine followed the Stoics in excluding animals from the moral community.

religion-illusion.rationale: Stoic physics is theology: the cosmos is ruled by a rational, providential god, and Diogenes Laertius says the wise honour the gods, pray and sacrifice to them while the godless man is bad, so religion as illusion contradicts the school.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The Stoics hold that a providential divine reason governs the world and that piety is a virtue (Diogenes Laertius, Epictetus), so a state promoting atheism would teach what they hold false; they do not say the state should teach religion.

nation-first.rationale: Moderate Stoic cosmopolitanism, as the Stanford article describes Cicero and Seneca, acknowledges obligations to one's own country in addition to those to the whole human community, and Cicero ranks country first among particular ties; it does not say which prevails in a conflict.

missingStatements.text: Only a person's moral character is good or bad; wealth, health and social standing are neither.
missingStatements.rationale: The defining Stoic thesis that virtue alone is good and other things are indifferents, stated in Diogenes Laertius and the Stanford article, shapes their views on wealth, power and the pursuit of status.

missingStatements.text: Every human being belongs to one community of reason, whatever state they live in.
missingStatements.rationale: Marcus Aurelius, Epictetus and Musonius call every person a citizen of one world city sharing reason and law, which the Stanford article presents as the core of Stoic cosmopolitanism.

missingStatements.text: A person should accept what lies outside their control and put their effort into their own judgments and conduct.
missingStatements.rationale: Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius build their ethics on this division between what is and is not in our power, and the Stanford and Internet encyclopedias present it as central.

missingStatements.text: Strong passions such as anger should be mastered by reason, not acted on.
missingStatements.rationale: Seneca's On Anger and Diogenes Laertius treat the passions as false judgements to be removed, and Seneca says justice and punishment are better carried out without anger.

Stoicism is a philosophy of life, not a political programme, so most modern policy statements are null. Searched by theme: government (constitution, kingship, law, tyranny, resistance, participation), world (cosmopolitanism, war, country), liberty and punishment (anger, mercy, execution, defence), society (family, sex, abortion, children, women's education, slavery), economy and property (Cicero on agrarian laws and debts, wealth as indifferent, simple living), nature and animals, religion. The Stoics did not agree on the best constitution (mixture, or monarchy for Seneca), on mercy, on sex outside marriage (Zeno's community of wives against Musonius), or on tyrannicide (Cicero against Seneca on Brutus). Musonius and Epictetus on women: Musonius says women and men should receive the same education in virtue but gives no position on the vote, property or law.
